passage:
You want to know why I quit the late shifts, Akash? It's me, Thomas, the guy who used to code for fun on Sundays. Last year I was on three projects at once. Twelve-hour days for eight months.
My body started falling apart. I caught every cold going around. My back ached. I was tired even after sleeping. And the worst part: I stopped caring about the work. I used to love it. Now I'd stare at the code and feel nothing.
I took a two-week holiday in Goa. Came back, and within three days I felt exactly the same.
That's when I realised a holiday wasn't the fix. The load was. I told my manager I couldn't do three projects. We cut it to one. I stopped answering messages after seven, saw my doctor about the colds, and started sleeping properly.
It's taken months. But last Sunday I opened my laptop and wrote something just for fun again.

qa.q: How many projects was Thomas on last year?
qa.a: Thomas was on three projects at once.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel about the work once loved so much?
qa.a: Thomas felt detached and empty, staring at the code and feeling nothing.

qa.q: What did Thomas realise after the holiday, and what changed?
qa.a: Thomas realised the load, not the lack of a holiday, was the problem, so the projects were cut to one, evening limits were set, a doctor was seen and sleep improved.

qa.q: How might Thomas's manager have felt on hearing that three projects were too many?
qa.a: The manager may have been surprised at first, but agreed to cut it to one, suggesting they valued Thomas staying well.

grounding: It shows a worker in long-term overload with tiredness, colds, aches and detachment, and how cutting the workload and resting helps more than a holiday.

passage:
I'm Pema. I teach at the same school as Kalyani, and I've shared the staff room with her for three years.
Kalyani used to be the loudest laugh in there. She ran the science club and stayed late to help students with projects. This year she took on exam duty, two extra classes and the annual day.
By December she always seemed to have a cold. She'd rub her lower back and sit with her eyes closed at lunch. When students came with project questions, she answered politely but flatly.
After the winter break she came back looking the same, pale and tired.
In January I saw her go into the principal's office. Afterwards her name was off the annual day list and one of the extra classes. I don't know everything she said. But last week she laughed in the staff room again, and it sounded like her.

qa.q: What extra work did Kalyani take on this year?
qa.a: She took on exam duty, two extra classes and the annual day.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have been feeling by December?
qa.a: She may have been exhausted and detached, though Pema can't be sure; she seemed tired, often ill and flat with students.

qa.q: What change seems to have helped Kalyani most?
qa.a: Talking to the principal and dropping the annual day and an extra class, since the break alone had not helped.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's students have experienced her in December?
qa.a: They probably noticed she was polite but flat, and may have missed her old warmth and energy.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, a teacher in long-term overload with colds, aches and detachment, who recovers after her workload is reduced rather than only after a holiday.
